final_proof:
Equip ℝ^d with its usual inner product ⟨x,y⟩ = ∑_{k=1}^d x_k y_k and the induced norm. First, this space is complete: if (x^(n)) is a Cauchy sequence in this norm, then, for each k, |x_k^(n) − x_k^(m)| ≤ ‖x^(n) − x^(m)‖, so (x_k^(n)) is a Cauchy sequence in ℝ. Let x_k be its limit and put x = (x_1,…,x_d). Since there are only finitely many coordinates, ‖x^(n) − x‖² = ∑_{k=1}^d |x_k^(n) − x_k|² → 0. Thus ℝ^d is indeed a Hilbert space.

For 1 ≤ i ≤ d, the standard vector e_i has kth coordinate δ_{ik}. Therefore, for all i and j,

⟨e_i,e_j⟩ = ∑_{k=1}^d δ_{ik}δ_{jk} = δ_{ij}.

Hence {e_1,…,e_d} is an orthonormal set. Now let x = (x_1,…,x_d) be arbitrary. Coordinatewise,

x = ∑_{i=1}^d x_i e_i.

Thus every vector in ℝ^d belongs to the linear span of {e_1,…,e_d}; consequently that span is all of ℝ^d and, in particular, its closure is all of ℝ^d. By the definition of a Hilbert-space basis as an orthonormal set with dense closed linear span, {e_1,…,e_d} is a basis of ℝ^d. Moreover, x_i = ⟨x,e_i⟩, so the displayed expansion also has the usual Fourier-coefficient form and is unique. (If d = 0 is allowed, the empty set is similarly an orthonormal basis of the zero Hilbert space, with the expansion interpreted as the empty sum.)
